sources: MacCulloch, J. A. The Religion of the Ancient Celts. London: Constable, 1911, 170.
Ross, Anne, and Michael Cyprien. *A Traveller’s Guide to Celtic Britain.* Harrisburg, Pa.: Historical Times, 1985, 67.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: For the Celts, the spirits of the dead stayed close to their families. The dead often remained inside the home, around the hearth. Their spirits were neutral or protective, but they needed regular care to stay beneficial. Honoring the ancestors may have been a form of worship in early Celtic life. The gods and goddesses stood as the mother and father of the tribe. In later, Christian times the reverence for a family’s own saint may descend from the same habit. In Brittany and other parts of France, people poured milk over graves, as though the dead needed food. In Ireland, on the day of Samhain, the boundary between this world and the Otherworld grew thin, and the dead returned to visit. They could sit in their favorite chairs, drink a cup, light a pipe, and warm themselves at the fire. The living left out food and tobacco for them. The rites carried a warning: if the dead were ignored, they could grow angry and disturb the world of the living.
